<pre><code></code></pre>
<h2><a id="user-content-dependencies" class="anchor" href="#dependencies" aria-hidden="true"><span class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>Dependencies</h2>

<p>This document depends on the following packages:</p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(<span class="pl-smi">devtools</span>)
  library(<span class="pl-smi">Biobase</span>)
})</pre></div>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>  library(<span class="pl-smi">devtools</span>)
  library(<span class="pl-smi">Biobase</span>)</pre></div>

<p>To install these packages you can use the code (or if you are compiling the document, remove the <code>eval=FALSE</code> from the chunk.)</p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>install.packages(c(<span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">"</span>devtools<span class="pl-pds">"</span></span>))
source(<span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">"</span>http://www.bioconductor.org/biocLite.R<span class="pl-pds">"</span></span>)
biocLite(c(<span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">"</span>Biobase<span class="pl-pds">"</span></span>))</pre></div>

<h2><a id="user-content-general-principles" class="anchor" href="#general-principles" aria-hidden="true"><span class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>General principles</h2>

<ul>
<li>Make sure data is on the right scale for

<ul>
<li>Visualization</li>
<li>Statistical modeling</li>
</ul></li>
</ul>

<h2><a id="user-content-load-some-data" class="anchor" href="#load-some-data" aria-hidden="true"><span class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>Load some data</h2>

<p>We will use this expression set to look at how we use plots and tables to check for different characteristics</p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre><span class="pl-v">con</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span>url(<span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">"</span>http://bowtie-bio.sourceforge.net/recount/ExpressionSets/bodymap_eset.RData<span class="pl-pds">"</span></span>)
load(<span class="pl-v">file</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-smi">con</span>)
close(<span class="pl-smi">con</span>)
<span class="pl-v">bm</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span> <span class="pl-smi">bodymap.eset</span>
<span class="pl-v">pdata</span><span class="pl-k">=</span>pData(<span class="pl-smi">bm</span>)
<span class="pl-v">edata</span><span class="pl-k">=</span>as.data.frame(exprs(<span class="pl-smi">bm</span>))
<span class="pl-v">fdata</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span> fData(<span class="pl-smi">bm</span>)
ls()</pre></div>

<h2><a id="user-content-skewed-distributions" class="anchor" href="#skewed-distributions" aria-hidden="true"><span class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>Skewed distributions</h2>

<p>We would like continuous data to be nice and summetric like a normal distribution for two reasons:(1) plots are easier to see this way and (2) most statistical methods are designed to work better for non-skewed data. </p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(rnorm(<span class="pl-c1">1000</span>),<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>)</pre></div>

<p>Realistically though most genomic data is skewed</p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>],<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>,<span class="pl-v">breaks</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">100</span>)</pre></div>

<p>One way to address this skew is to use a transformation. One common transformation is the <code>log</code> transform. </p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(log(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>]),<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>,<span class="pl-v">breaks</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">100</span>)</pre></div>

<p>One thing to be careful with is that values of zero become <code>-inf</code> when you apply the log transform because the log of zero isn't defined. </p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>min(log(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>))</pre></div>

<p>You can remove this problem by adding a small number to all the counts before taking the log. This doesn't change the overall distribution much but resolves the zero problem</p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>min(log(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>] <span class="pl-k">+</span> <span class="pl-c1">1</span>))
hist(log(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>] <span class="pl-k">+</span> <span class="pl-c1">1</span>),<span class="pl-v">breaks</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">100</span>,<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>)</pre></div>

<p>A common choice is to use the <code>log2</code> transform. The reason is that data on the <code>log2</code> scale can be expressed as <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fold_change">fold changes</a>. If <code>log2(x) - log2(y) = z</code> then there is a <code>z</code> fold change difference between <code>x</code> and <code>y</code>. </p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(log2(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>] <span class="pl-k">+</span> <span class="pl-c1">1</span>),<span class="pl-v">breaks</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">100</span>,<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>)</pre></div>

<p>Let's zoom in on the values greater than zero (we'll come back to the zero values in a minute)</p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(log2(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>] <span class="pl-k">+</span> <span class="pl-c1">1</span>),<span class="pl-v">breaks</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">100</span>,<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>,<span class="pl-v">xlim</span><span class="pl-k">=</span>c(<span class="pl-c1">1</span>,<span class="pl-c1">15</span>),<span class="pl-v">ylim</span><span class="pl-k">=</span>c(<span class="pl-c1">0</span>,<span class="pl-c1">400</span>))</pre></div>

<p>This is starting to look a little better but we still have the zeros problem. </p>

<h2><a id="user-content-removing-features-without-much-data" class="anchor" href="#removing-features-without-much-data" aria-hidden="true"><span class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>Removing features without much data</h2>

<p>In many types of sequencing data we observe that there is not much data for many features. </p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(rowSums(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span><span class="pl-k">==</span><span class="pl-c1">0</span>),<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>)</pre></div>

<p>A common pre-processing technique is to remove features that don't have much data. One way to identify and remove them is to use <code>rowMeans</code> and <code>rowMedians</code></p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre><span class="pl-v">low_genes</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span> rowMeans(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>) <span class="pl-k">&lt;</span> <span class="pl-c1">5</span>
table(<span class="pl-smi">low_genes</span>)
<span class="pl-v">filt_edata</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span> filter(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>,<span class="pl-k">!</span><span class="pl-smi">low_genes</span>)
dim(<span class="pl-smi">filt_edata</span>)

<span class="pl-v">low_genes2</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span> rowMedians(as.matrix(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>)) <span class="pl-k">&lt;</span> <span class="pl-c1">5</span>
table(<span class="pl-smi">low_genes2</span>,<span class="pl-smi">low_genes</span>)
<span class="pl-v">filt_edata2</span> <span class="pl-k">=</span> filter(<span class="pl-smi">edata</span>,<span class="pl-k">!</span><span class="pl-smi">low_genes2</span>)
dim(<span class="pl-smi">filt_edata2</span>)</pre></div>

<p>After filtering we observe that using the <code>log</code> transform makes the distribution much more symmetric but there are still zeros. We could increase the filter to remove this issue if we needed to. </p>

<div class="highlight highlight-r"><pre>hist(log2(<span class="pl-smi">filt_edata</span>[,<span class="pl-c1">1</span>] <span class="pl-k">+</span> <span class="pl-c1">1</span>),<span class="pl-v">col</span><span class="pl-k">=</span><span class="pl-c1">2</span>)</pre></div>

<h2><a id="user-content-more-transforms" class="anchor" href="#more-transforms" aria-hidden="true"><span class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>More transforms</h2>

<p>There are a large number of other transforms depending on the type of data you are using. Some common ones are:</p>

<ul>
<li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance-stabilizing_transformation">Variance stabilizing transforms</a> which seek to remove a mean variance relationship among the data</li>
<li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_transform">Box-Cox transforms</a> which seek to make the data approximately Normally distributed</li>
<li><a href="http://rpackages.ianhowson.com/bioc/DESeq2/man/rlog.html">rlog transform</a> - unique to genomics count data, this is a regularized version of the log transform that seeks to minimize differences at low count levels. </li>
</ul>
